task_statement:
Research question (as posed on 2026-11-02, in the area of lineup and matchup effects):
Changing the offensive five itself moves shot mix, showing the design can detect personnel effects.

Data available on that date:
- NBA 2022-23 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2023-24 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2024-25 regular season and playoffs
- Sources: Per-game files from the NBA stats API: play-by-play (action type, sub-type, clock, period, score, player, shot distance and result), substitution rotation intervals, starters, defensive matchup minutes and partial possessions, box-score summary. Derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database built from the play-by-play.

Your job is to decide, before any analysis is run, whether this question can be answered with this data, what has already been established about it, which methodological and statistical risks threaten a test of it, and either a pre-registration-quality design or a reasoned recommendation not to proceed.

methodological_questions: identification of offensive lineup effect on shot mix
control for opponent lineup and team quality

historical_evidence.finding: Offenses attack the rim more when the opponent has no big on the floor, with observed increases in DRIVE (+0.82pp) and POST_UP (+0.43pp) and a decrease in 3PA (-1.79pp). The evidence was inconclusive due to limited sample and power.
Sequence-memory lag effects were found to be an artifact; observed lift effects collapsed when within-team baselines were applied.
Lag‑1 play‑type PPP effects disappeared after adding game‑state controls, indicating the original effects were artifacts.
Offenses did not reliably tilt play‑type mix toward opponent defensive weaknesses; the observed tilt had the wrong sign and was not statistically significant.

failed_approaches.why: C_artifact (apparent effect produced by construction or labeling flaw)

failed_approaches.what_failed: Lag‑1 PPP effect estimation with game‑state controls
failed_approaches.why: C_artifact (apparent effect produced by construction or labeling flaw)

failed_approaches.what_failed: Game‑plan adaptation to opponent prior defensive weakness
Opponent lineup adaptation effect on shot mix
failed_approaches.why: SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER (limited sample and power leading to inconclusive results)

evidence_establishes: There is some evidence that changes in the opponent lineup (specifically the presence or absence of rim defenders) can affect an offensive team's shot mix, but these effects were inconclusive and potentially small.
evidence_does_not_establish: No empirical evidence directly shows that changing the offensive lineup itself causes a detectable shift in shot mix. Existing studies have focused on opponent lineup changes or game‑plan adaptation, not on the offensive personnel effect.
own_inferences: The data provide a large number of possessions across three seasons, which should allow estimation of shot‑mix changes associated with offensive lineup changes, but the effect size may be small and exposure sparsity could limit power. The design must carefully control for opponent lineup, team quality, and game context to isolate the offensive lineup effect.
uncertainties: Whether the sample of offensive lineup changes is sufficiently large and diverse to detect small effect sizes; the reliability of shot‑type classification across seasons; potential confounding by coaching strategies that co‑vary with lineup changes.

historical_effect.explanation: The historical evidence indicates that while opponent lineup changes can influence shot mix, the effect size is small and results are inconclusive, suggesting that detecting offensive lineup effects will be challenging but not impossible. This tempered confidence leads to a decision to proceed with methodological safeguards.

blocking_constraints.text: Limited power to detect small effect sizes with many offensive lineup categories.
Some lineups occur rarely, reducing exposure for those groups.
Shot‑type classification may have measurement error, especially across seasons.
Team quality, opponent lineup, and game state may confound the relationship between offensive lineup and shot mix.

prior_work.summary: No prior study has conclusively shown that changing the offensive lineup itself alters shot mix; the only related evidence concerns opponent lineup changes and is inconclusive.

risks.text: Large number of offensive lineup categories may dilute power to detect effects.
Some lineups are rarely used, limiting data for those groups.
Shot‑type classification may vary across seasons, introducing measurement error.
Team quality and opponent lineup can simultaneously affect shot mix.

design.estimand: Change in offensive shot‑mix proportions attributable to a change in the offensive lineup, net of opponent lineup and team quality.
design.sample: All games from 2022‑23 to 2024‑25 where the offensive lineup changed relative to the previous game or a matched control game.
design.power: Target 80% power to detect a 0.6pp shift in a dominant shot type (e.g., DRIVE) with α=0.05 (two‑sided), requiring ~400 games with sufficient exposure per lineup category.
design.controls: Fixed effects for team, opponent, game context (home/away, back‑to‑back, score margin), and opponent lineup composition; matched‑pairs design controlling for opponent lineup on the day of the offensive lineup change.
design.falsification: Test whether the same effect appears when the offensive lineup changes but the opponent lineup and game context remain identical; also test a placebo period with no lineup change to verify no spurious shifts.
design.multiplicity: Pre‑registered primary outcome (overall shot mix proportion). Secondary outcomes (individual play types) will be tested with Holm-Bonferroni correction. All analyses will be performed in the same statistical software environment with version control.
design.decision_rule: Reject null if p<0.05 for overall shot‑mix shift; otherwise report effect size and confidence interval. If power is insufficient for specific lineup categories, report aggregated effect across similar lineups.
design.data_version: NBA 2022‑23 regular season and playoffs, 2023‑24 regular season and playoffs, 2024‑25 regular season and playoffs (per‑game play‑by‑play and derived possession data).
